reading.title: A Field Guide to Classic Poetic Forms
reading.purpose: Learn how different poetic forms use rhythm and structure to shape emotion.
paras: Poems may look short on the page, yet their shapes are built with care. Long before books were printed, listeners remembered verses by their meter, the steady beat of stressed and unstressed syllables that gives lines a musical pulse. A poet chooses a form the way a musician chooses an instrument, matching sound and structure to the feeling of the subject.

Some forms are built to tell tales. A ballad is a story-telling poem or song arranged in short verses that move quickly from scene to scene, often about sea voyages, heroes, or quiet village mysteries. Other poems focus on inner emotion rather than plot. A lyric poem expresses personal feelings in a song-like voice, letting a reader step inside a single moment of joy, wonder, or doubt.

Strict rules can sharpen a writer's craft. A sonnet packs an entire argument or reflection into exactly fourteen lines with a set rhyme pattern. Because space is tight, every image must carry real weight. When a poet writes an elegy, a poem of sorrow mourning someone who has died, the measured pace invites readers to pause and contemplate loss deeply rather than rushing past it.

Word choice gives each form its final color. Some poets favor warm sentiment, sharing tender feelings openly in clear, musical phrases. Others prefer stark lines—bare, plain, and unsoftened—like winter branches against a gray sky. When rhythm and honest images work together, a poem can feel deeply poignant, stirring tender sadness, or even haunting, lingering in a reader's memory long after the book is closed.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "elegy" most nearly means
choices: a fast song about a sailor crossing a stormy sea
a poem of sorrow written to mourn someone who has died
a fourteen-line puzzle that ends with a funny twist
a list of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line
qs.why: Paragraph 3 defines elegy directly as "a poem of sorrow mourning someone who has died."

qs.q: Which sentence explains how a lyric poem differs from a story-telling ballad?
choices: Some forms are built to tell tales.
A ballad is a story-telling poem or song arranged in short verses that move quickly from scene to scene, often about sea voyages, heroes, or quiet village mysteries.
Other poems focus on inner emotion rather than plot.
A lyric poem expresses personal feelings in a song-like voice, letting a reader step inside a single moment of joy, wonder, or doubt.
qs.why: This sentence describes what a lyric poem does: expressing personal feelings in a song-like voice instead of telling a multi-scene story.

ev.text: A lyric poem expresses personal feelings in a song-like voice, letting a reader step inside a single moment of joy, wonder, or doubt.

qs.q: Why must every image carry real weight inside a sonnet?
choices: The form limits the poet to fourteen lines, leaving no room for wasted words.
Readers refuse to read any poem that has fewer than three rhyming verses.
Sonnets are always sung aloud without any steady pattern of stressed beats.
Poets are not allowed to mention winter branches or natural scenes in them.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 explains that a sonnet packs an argument or reflection into exactly fourteen lines, so space is tight.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Modern poets no longer need rhythm or rhyme because printed books are easy to buy.
Ballads are more enjoyable than elegies because they focus on exciting sea voyages.
Poets pair specific forms, rhythms, and word choices to create lasting emotional effects.
Every classic poem must use bare, harsh language in order to stay in a reader's mind.
qs.why: The reading surveys meter, ballads, lyric poems, sonnets, elegies, and word choices to show how structure shapes feeling.
